chapters.title: Living With Wildfire in Homestead Valley
chapters.description: For generations, Homestead Valley residents have worked together to preserve something unique and extraordinary — a mountain village community where homes, forests, ridgelines and open space exist side by side, just twenty minutes from San Francisco.

chapters.title: A Landscape Worth Protecting
chapters.description:
For generations, Homestead Valley residents have worked together to preserve something unique and extraordinary — a mountain village community where homes, forests, ridgelines and open space exist side by side.

Like living in Telluride, but just twenty minutes from San Francisco.

We live here because of that landscape, because of the natural setting. It is part of what makes Homestead Valley beautiful, distinctive and valuable.

chapters.title: This Is Also Our Risk
chapters.description:
It is also a big part of our elevated wildfire risk.

The threat wildfire poses to life and safety is very real, even if a catastrophic fire can feel distant or abstract somehow — “something that happens to someone else.” It has happened all around us, and it can happen here.

Wildfire also presents a more immediate and tangible concern: the potential for catastrophic financial loss — to affected victims obviously, but also to neighbors whose homes didn't burn. Consequences don't end when the fire is extinguished. Affected families are often displaced for years. Properties need to be decontaminated. Insurance and rebuilding get mired in permits, hearings, disputes and appeals. There aren't enough contractors to rebuild quickly.

The fact is that the financial effects of a catastrophic wildfire ripple across an entire community for a decade.

That is why wildfire resilience matters now — not only because of what could happen during a wildfire, but because of what wildfire risk already means for homeowners and communities.

We are protecting more than structures. We are protecting people, homes, financial security, and the ongoing viability of the special community we have inherited.

The good news is that wildfire risk is not simply something that happens to us. There are meaningful things we can do — individually and together — to influence what happens when wildfire reaches our community. In fact there is a lot we are already doing, and a history of activism and preservation that we can be proud of, but that it is now time to build upon.

Wildfire is a natural part of our environment. Whether or not we become victims depends a great deal on the preparation we take, along with our neighbors.

media.alt: Chart breaking large-scale wildfire recovery into six categories of action: debris removal, residential rebuilding, commercial and economic recovery, public infrastructure, community facilities and services, and environmental restoration
media.caption: Recovery is not one task. Source: California Disaster Recovery Framework, Cal OES; National Disaster Recovery Framework, FEMA.

media.caption: Historical reconstruction rates suggest five years to rebuild half of a community's homes, and eleven to reach 70%. Source: McKinsey & Company.

chapters.title: Homestead Valley Within Marin County
chapters.description: Zoom out, and Homestead Valley — shown here in red — is a small piece of a much larger county. We sit in Southern Marin, between Mill Valley and Mount Tamalpais State Park, part of one of California's most beautiful, and most wildfire-prone, landscapes. Officially, our community is Marin County Service Area 14 (CSA 14): a roughly 469-acre district that the County and local fire agencies use to define Homestead Valley's boundary.

chapters.title: We Are Not Starting From Scratch
chapters.description:
A community preparing for the future.

Wildfire resilience in Homestead Valley did not begin with recent fires or changing insurance markets. It has been developing for nearly two decades through the work of residents, volunteers, community organizations, local fire agencies and public partners.

As our understanding of wildfire risk has evolved, so too has our community's response.

Today, Homestead Valley benefits from years of planning, leadership, successful grant funding, neighborhood organization, and ongoing investment in reducing wildfire risk.

media.alt: Panoramic view across a Homestead Valley neighborhood with Mount Tamalpais on the skyline
media.caption: Building a more resilient Homestead Valley.

chapters.title: Where We Are Today
chapters.description:
Thousands of home assessments conducted by the Southern Marin Fire District, together with observations documented through the Homestead Valley Firewise USA Community Wildfire Risk Assessment, provide a clear picture of where our community stands today.

The results are encouraging.

Homestead was one of Marin's first Firewise communities, and as neighbors we continue to invest in resilience at our homes. Over the past decade we have made measurable progress on a number of fronts: most homes now have Class A roofs, metal gutters are common, roof maintenance has improved considerably, the fire department is very proactive in conducting inspections, and our tax dollars support the Marin Wildfire Prevention Authority.

These improvements significantly reduce the likelihood that homes will ignite during an ember storm.

media.alt: NFPA Firewise USA logo with the tagline: residents reducing wildfire risks
media.caption: Homestead Valley was one of Marin County's first Firewise USA communities.

media.alt: Steve Quarles on building materials, roofs and ember resistance
media.caption: Steve Quarles — what a decade of home hardening has actually bought us.

chapters.title: The Same Assessments Show Our Greatest Opportunities
chapters.description:
California has recently released the approved Zone Zero defensible space regulations.

Upgrading ember-resistant vents, reducing the vulnerabilities associated with combustible decks and fence connections, and continuing thoughtful vegetation management remain the most impactful actions available to us today.

Let's not let the perfect become the enemy of the good, though. Start small and get going.

Wildfire resilience is built through hundreds of practical improvements, completed over time, by hundreds of homeowners working toward the same goal.

media.alt: Before and after comparison of the first five feet around a home: a vulnerable side yard with a wood fence, wood mulch and shrubs against the siding, versus a Zone 0 compliant yard with a metal gate, gravel ground cover and plants set back five feet
media.caption: Zone 0 — the first five feet. Non-combustible alternatives include gravel, decomposed granite, pavers and concrete.

chapters.title: The Next Frontier: Neighborhood Resilience
chapters.description:
For many years wildfire preparedness focused on a single question: “How can I protect my home?” — or perhaps “How can I hang on to my homeowner's policy, or get off the FAIR Plan?”

We've just talked about individual homes. But the story gets a lot more interesting once a volume of neighbors get together to harden their homes.

“How can we protect our immediate neighborhood?”

When 70% of homes in a neighborhood are hardened, the chances of catastrophic conflagration go down significantly. As each home is hardened there is less chance it will turn into fuel, throwing massive embers at the homes next door.

Wildfire does not recognize property lines. Embers travel freely between homes. Vegetation crosses property lines. Wood fences connect structures. One vulnerable home can threaten many others — and likewise, one well-prepared home benefits when its surrounding neighbors have also reduced their vulnerabilities.

This is one of the most important shifts occurring in wildfire mitigation today, and home insurers are paying attention. Sometimes their recommendations differ a little from the fire agencies' — see, for example, Mercury Insurance's California home hardening self-assessment.

Increasingly, wildfire resilience — and increasingly, community insurability — is being viewed as a neighborhood challenge rather than simply an individual responsibility.

While no single mitigation project or community designation guarantees insurance coverage or meaningful premium savings, insurers and regulators are paying greater attention to documented individual and community investment in wildfire risk reduction. It is not so much about reducing premiums as it is about remaining insurable, and not being relegated to the FAIR Plan.

Programs such as Firewise USA, California's Safer from Wildfires initiative and neighborhood-scale mitigation efforts demonstrate that communities are actively working together to reduce wildfire exposure.

The stronger the neighborhood, the stronger every home within it becomes.

chapters.title: Fostering a Culture of Preparedness
chapters.description:
We have a history of proactive neighbors who have taken steps to create and protect the Homestead Valley we enjoy today.

The Homestead Valley Safety Committee was formed in 2010 with a primary focus on earthquake preparedness. Originally known as the Emergency Response Group (ERG), the committee organized Homestead Valley into 69 neighborhood blocks, each served by a volunteer Block Captain.

Block Captains developed neighborhood contact lists, identified neighbors who might require additional assistance during emergencies, established evacuation procedures and created neighborhood communication networks. The Safety Committee continues today through the Neighborhood Response Group (NRG), with radio exercises conducted twice each year.

Much of this work has been led by Jim Derich, who succeeded Robert Hunn as committee chair around 2010. A longtime Mill Valley educator and elementary school principal, Jim brought decades of emergency planning experience to Homestead Valley. Following the North Bay wildfires between 2017 and 2020, he helped guide the committee's transition from earthquake preparedness toward a greater focus on wildfire resilience.

Today the Safety Committee coordinates our Firewise activities, including managing the comprehensive home hardening measures taken over the last year at the Community Center — which serve as an example to community members of the steps we can all take at our own homes.

chapters.title: Firewise: Turning Planning Into Action
chapters.description:
As Homestead Valley prepared to become one of Marin County's first Firewise Communities, then Fire Captain Corey Gloeckner of Southern Marin Fire District completed a comprehensive wildfire assessment. The report established the technical foundation for Homestead Valley's Firewise designation and identified priorities for reducing community wildfire risk.

Read the full Firewise assessment report (PDF)

Firewise recognition also helped secure two initial wildfire mitigation grants totaling an impressive approximately $400,000.

These funds supported major fuel reduction projects — particularly thinning the eucalyptus groves surrounding residential neighborhoods — as well as launching the community-wide reflective address placard program, improving emergency responders' ability to quickly locate homes during emergencies.

More than 500 of approximately 900 homes have now installed reflective address placards.

Community preparedness continues to evolve. Recent investments have hardened the Homestead Valley Community Center as both a demonstration project for wildfire resilience and an emergency resource for the community. Current efforts focus on expanding Neighborhood Response Groups, improving emergency communications, strengthening neighborhood coordination and continuing public education through regular newsletters and outreach.

Southern Marin Fire District is a proactive partner to Homestead Valley, conducting hundreds of annual home inspections with wildfire risk reports and supporting HVLT's open space fuel management efforts with budget and work crews.

chapters.title: A Foundation of Preservation — How Do We Grow It?
chapters.description:
We have a history in Homestead of community activation that goes back well before Firewise, and even before the Homestead Valley Safety Committee.

Over 50 years ago, Homestead community members had the foresight and the expertise to organize their neighbors and raise money through a bond issue — quite literally creating the Homestead Valley that we enjoy today by setting aside close to 100 acres, and establishing and maintaining the copious hiking trails and the majestic Stolte and Three Groves. You can read more in the Homestead Valley Land Trust's own history.

This work demonstrates an important lesson:

Meaningful change is possible. It's built through vision, leadership, community engagement and sustained effort.

The volunteers who organized neighborhoods, the residents who secured grants, the organizations that steward our open space and the public agencies that continue to invest in wildfire mitigation have created a strong foundation for Homestead's future.

Ironically, some of what we think we know about wildfire may actually make the problem seem more overwhelming than it is.

What would wildfire really look like if it reached Homestead Valley? Is the greatest threat a wall of flames — or something much smaller? What can you do around your own property to influence the outcome? And what becomes possible when neighbors begin doing those things together?

Pro Tip: Start With What You Can ControlYou cannot control where a wildfire starts or which way the wind blows. Focus first on the conditions around your home and neighborhood that you can change.

chapters.title: What Does Wildfire Mean Here?
chapters.description:
When most of us picture wildfire, we imagine a forest or brush fire burning out of control in the mountains — or perhaps a wall of flames advancing toward homes over a distant ridge.

That can happen.

But in a community like Homestead Valley, the greater concern is what happens when wildfire enters the built environment.

Wind-driven embers will often travel well ahead of a fire, exposing many properties at once. If those embers — or an approaching fire — ignite homes, vegetation, fences, decks or other combustible materials, the emergency spirals out of control as one ignition explodes in embers and contributes to another, until emergency responders lose control.

A wildfire has become a neighborhood fire.

Once multiple structures are burning, emergency resources will quickly become stretched. Firefighters will focus on evacuation, life safety and containing the larger fire rather than defending individual homes.

chapters.title: Why Homestead Is Different
chapters.description:
Our exposure is shaped by the landscape around us — the extraordinary beauty we enjoy every day.

Homestead occupies a landscape of ridges, steep slopes, valleys and drainages. Our homes sit alongside a larger network of HVLT, Marin County and federal open space.

Some homes sit high on ridgelines reached by narrow, winding roads, characterized by high winds and neighboring homes within 20 feet of one another. Others are nestled in valleys or drainages. Still others are high in the hills on cul-de-sac roads, backing directly onto HVLT open space. Some of us live near the eucalyptus groves on the Pixie side of the valley, or across, above the bee boxes on the Homestead Trail.

These are not abstract conditions on a hazard map. They are the ridges we see from our windows, the trees that surround us, the open spaces we shepherd as a community and the trails we walk every day.

This is the landscape we have chosen to live in. The question is not how to eliminate wildfire from it, but how to live more resiliently within it.
Pro Tip: Know Your ExposureLook at where your home sits within Homestead. Are you below a ridge, above a drainage, beside open space, or on a narrow hillside road? Your location helps determine where to focus first.

media.alt: Framework showing how terrain exposure (ridge or steep slope versus gentle slope) and surroundings (open space versus developed lots) combine into four exposure profiles, each with a different mitigation focus
media.caption: Understanding your home's risk — four exposure profiles, four different places to start.

chapters.title: See the Shape of Homestead
chapters.description:
Our exposure begins with the landscape itself.

Homestead is not a flat suburban grid. Ridgelines, steep slopes, valleys and drainages shape both how fire moves and how we move — the terrain itself shapes fire behavior and access.

media.alt: Infographic showing how slope, canyons and wind drive wildfire spread across Homestead's terrain
media.caption: How slope, canyons and southwest aspect drive wildfire spread.

chapters.mapNote: Elevation shown here is real USGS 3DEP 1m LIDAR-derived terrain (see topo_work/), classed into the same 8 hypsometric-tint bands used in the topography graphic above. The relief shading over it is computed from the same 1m DEM and clipped to the CSA 14 boundary. Separate slope/aspect layers remain in that graphic only.

chapters.title: See the Wildland-Urban Interface
chapters.description:
Our homes sit within and beside a much larger landscape.

Homestead's neighborhoods sit closely interwoven with HVLT open space, Marin County lands, GGNRA and the CSA 14 service-area boundary — this is what makes us a wildland-urban interface community.

media.alt: Definition of the wildland-urban interface (WUI)

chapters.mapNote: Vegetation density shown here (from Sentinel-2 NDVI analysis) is a real, data-derived proxy for fuel load across the wildland-urban interface, with relief shading from the 1m LIDAR DEM over it. Gaps in the green are ground that scored below the vegetated threshold on a September dry-season scene — roads, roofs and cured grass — not missing data. HVLT open space, Marin County lands and GGNRA boundaries are not yet available as GIS layers from the client, so they are not shown.

chapters.title: See How Wind Can Change Exposure
chapters.description:
Wind can change which parts of Homestead are most exposed.

While wind can vary, there are two primary wind and weather events that create the greatest risk in Homestead, and they are usually present on red flag days: a Diablo, offshore wind event, and a reverse, onshore or southwest wind. Each exposes a different part of the community.

There is no single direction from which wildfire must arrive.

media.alt: Infographic comparing Diablo/offshore wind events and reverse/onshore (southwest) wind events in Homestead Valley
media.caption: Diablo/offshore wind vs. reverse/onshore (southwest) wind scenarios.

chapters.mapNote: Diablo (offshore) and reverse (onshore) wind arrows are schematic direction indicators, not a meteorological model.

chapters.title: See the Access Challenge
chapters.description:
Terrain also shapes our ability to evacuate — and firefighters' ability to reach us.

Most of our streets are narrow and winding. If there is a fire at higher elevation and neighbors are evacuating while first responders are trying to reach the incident, traffic and access could further complicate matters.

Winding hillside streets, ridgeline roads, dead ends, cul-de-sacs and limited access and egress areas all mean the same thing:

Structure defense cannot always be assumed during a fast-moving incident.
chapters.mapNote: Elevation contours (20 ft interval, labeled every 40 ft) show the terrain evacuation routes have to climb. Road network distinguishes through-streets (solid) from service drives, footpaths and trails (dotted) — the routes actually available for evacuation and fire-apparatus access.

chapters.title: See the Landscape We Know
chapters.description:
These aren't abstract risks. This is the landscape we use every day.

The HVLT trail system, familiar trailheads, ridges and open-space areas move us from "here is a wildfire-risk map" to "I know these trails. I know that ridge. That's behind my neighborhood."

media.alt: Homestead Valley Land Trust trail map showing the trail network, trailheads and adjacent open space
media.caption: The HVLT trail network.

chapters.mapNote: Trail overlay shown is a placeholder — final version will show the HVLT trail system with labeled trailheads and ridges.

chapters.title: Where Do We Have the Greatest Ability to Intervene?
chapters.description:
This is the landscape we have chosen to live in. The question is not how to eliminate wildfire from it, but how to live more resiliently within it.

If the goal is to prevent wildfire from becoming a neighborhood fire, where do we have the greatest ability to intervene?

The answer begins with understanding how homes actually ignite.
chapters.mapNote: Fuel load and elevation are mapped together as a bivariate surface: red intensifies with vegetation density, blue with elevation, and the two combine to dark plum where both are high — the ground where fuel treatment and access work pay off most. Pale neutral means neither factor is elevated. Read any color off the 4×4 legend grid to recover both values.

chapters.title: Analyze My Own Block
chapters.description:
So much of our risk is associated with the way our homes sit in their natural setting — the topography, the aspect, the prevailing winds.

Which means the county-wide view only takes you so far. The next step is to zoom all the way in, to your street, with the same layers you have just been reading at the community scale.

Keep scrolling — the Block Explorer below lets you do exactly that.
chapters.mapNote: Scroll on to the Block Explorer to move from this community-wide view down to the block level, with the same terrain, vegetation and street layers available there.

chapters.title: How Homes Ignite: Embers Find a Way
chapters.description:
When most of us imagine wildfire threatening a home, we picture a wall of flames moving through the landscape toward us.

But a wildfire does not have to reach your home for your home to ignite.

Wind-driven embers can travel well ahead of the main fire. During a major wind event, thousands of embers can cross ridges and neighborhoods before the flame front arrives.

Most will burn out harmlessly. The ones that matter are those that find something receptive to burn.

Embers can collect in gutters and beneath decks, enter vulnerable vents and openings, or ignite dry vegetation, leaf litter, wood mulch and other combustible materials around a home. Those initial spot fires can then expose windows, siding, decks, fences and ultimately the structure itself.

Once a home ignites, the equation changes. The structure becomes another source of heat, flame and embers capable of threatening neighboring properties.

That is one way a wildfire becomes a neighborhood fire.

media.alt: Infographic titled Embers Travel Far Ahead, showing embers carried by wind up to five miles ahead of the main fire front, five common ways embers ignite homes (roofs and gutters, vents, decks and patios, eaves and siding, landscaping), and five defensive actions
media.caption: Embers can ignite homes without any direct flame contact — travelling one to five miles ahead of the fire front, and in rare cases farther.

chapters.title: A Different Way to Think About the Threat
chapters.description:
This distinction matters because it changes the problem from something that can feel overwhelming — stopping a wildfire — to something much more actionable: preventing an ember from becoming an ignition.

We cannot control where every ember will travel. But we can influence what those embers find when they arrive.

If thousands of embers landed on and around your home today, what would they find?

That question brings wildfire resilience down to the scale of our own homes and properties — and to things we can actually change. It leads to two complementary ways of thinking about reducing our risk:

First, reduce the vulnerabilities that allow embers to ignite our homes. Second, de-energize the pathways that can carry fire toward them.

chapters.title: The Fire Can Arrive Before the Flames
chapters.description:
A wildfire does not have to reach your home for your home to ignite.

Wind-driven embers can jump ridges and ignite homes well ahead of the main fire, carried by strong Diablo winds.

media.alt: Infographic: a flame front, Diablo winds lifting embers over a ridge, and resulting spot ignitions roughly 1.5-2 miles away in another neighborhood
media.caption: 1.5–2 miles is an illustrative ember-travel distance, not a hard maximum — embers can travel farther under the right wind conditions.

chapters.title: From Ember to Neighborhood Fire
chapters.description:
Fire front. Ember front. Spot ignitions. Structure ignition. Neighborhood conflagration.

Thousands of embers over time + something receptive to burn = ignition.

If thousands of embers landed on and around your home today, what would they find?

media.src: media/Embers Move In Front of Flames.png
media.alt: Five-stage sequence: fire front, ember front, spot ignitions, structure ignition, neighborhood conflagration
media.caption: The five-stage sequence from fire front to neighborhood conflagration.

chapters.title: Where Would an Ember Find a Way In?
chapters.description:
Roof and gutters. Vents. Eaves. Windows. Zone 0 vegetation. Combustible mulch and debris. Decks and under-deck areas. Fence connections. Foundation vents protected with 1/8-inch-or-less mesh. A six-inch noncombustible separation at grade.

Small changes at these entry points make a big difference.

media.alt: Home hardening details graphic showing ember entry points: roof/gutters, vents, eaves, windows, Zone 0, deck, under-deck, fence connections, foundation vents
media.caption: Home hardening details: where an ember could find a way in.

chapters.title: Same Home. Different Outcome.
chapters.description:
Ember Vulnerable — wood mulch, vegetation against the structure, debris accumulation, vulnerable vents and openings, combustible connections.

Ember Ready — gravel or noncombustible Zone 0, separated vegetation, screened vents, protected gutters, enclosed under-deck areas and reduced ember-entry opportunities.

The "after" home is still attractive, green and recognizably Homestead. Wildfire resilience doesn't mean stripping your property bare — it means being strategic about where and how fuels occur.

media.src: media/High risk home vs. low risk.png
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison of a high risk, ember-vulnerable home and a low risk, ember-ready home
media.caption: Same home, different outcome — small changes at entry points make a big difference.

chapters.title: Two Ways to Reduce Our Risk
chapters.description:
We cannot control the wind. We cannot control the terrain. And we cannot control where every ember will land.

But we can change the conditions those embers encounter — and the pathways a fire can use to reach our homes.

DE-ENERGIZE THE FIRE.
HARDEN THE HOME.

chapters.title: Two Ways to Reduce Our Risk
chapters.description:
Wildfire risk is shaped by factors we cannot control — terrain, weather and where a fire starts.

But we can influence how fire behaves as it approaches our homes and what happens when embers arrive. Think about that in two ways:

chapters.title: De-Energize an Approaching Fire by Reducing Laddering Opportunities
chapters.description:
Vegetation can either carry fire toward a home or help slow it down.

On a slope, continuous grasses, shrubs, trees and other fuels can create pathways for fire to climb toward structures. By thinning vegetation, eliminating ladder fuels and creating separation between groups of plants and trees, we can interrupt those pathways and reduce the energy available to the fire.

The goal is not to eliminate vegetation. It is to manage and maintain it strategically around the home so that an approaching fire has less fuel, is directed away from the home and burns with less intensity.

Pro Tip: Think Like an EmberWalk around your house and ask: Where could an ember land, collect, get inside, or ignite something? Small gaps and small accumulations can matter.

media.alt: Side-by-side hillside scenarios: an untreated home with continuous fire pathways under Diablo wind versus a treated, de-energized home with interrupted fuel breaks, same 25-degree slope
media.caption: Vegetation management interrupts the fire pathway, even under the same slope, fuel and Diablo-wind conditions.

chapters.title: Harden Your Home Against Embers
chapters.description:
At the same time, assume that embers will arrive.

Look at the home and its immediate surroundings through the eyes of an ember: vents, gutters, eaves, decks, fences, windows, debris and combustible materials close to the structure.

The goal is simple: give embers fewer opportunities to become ignitions.

media.alt: Combined infographic: de-energizing an approaching fire pathway (top) and preparing a home against embers, before and after (bottom)
media.caption: Look outward to de-energize the fire, look inward to make the home ember ready.

chapters.title: Two Strategies. One Objective.
chapters.description:
De-energize the pathways approaching the home. Harden the home against the embers that get there.

Neither eliminates wildfire risk. Together, they can significantly change the conditions a wildfire encounters.

And that brings the focus to the area where many of those conditions come together:

The space immediately surrounding our homes.

chapters.title: Start Closest to Home
chapters.description:
The closer combustible material is to your home, the greater the opportunity for a small ignition to threaten the structure.

That is why defensible space is organized into zones.

chapters.title: Zone 0 — 0 to 5 Feet: Start Here
chapters.description:
Think of Zone 0 as your home's first line of defense against ignition.

The first five feet around the home deserve special attention because a spot fire from an ember landing here has very little distance to travel before threatening the structure.

Keep this area lean, clean and as noncombustible as practical. Remove accumulated leaves and debris. Reduce vegetation immediately against the home to well-irrigated plants — succulents ideally, no taller than 18 inches. Replace combustible mulch where appropriate, and pay particular attention to anything that connects directly to the structure: gates, fences, decks, stairs and other combustible materials.

And look up. Trees are fine inside Zone 0 as long as their under-canopy is at least 7 feet above the roof line.

California has now released the approved Zone 0, 1 and 2 defensible space regulations — worth reading before you start.

media.alt: Before and after comparison of the first five feet around a home: a vulnerable side yard with a wood fence, wood mulch and shrubs against the siding, versus a Zone 0 compliant yard with a metal gate, gravel ground cover and plants set back five feet
media.caption: Zone 0 before and after — and the non-combustible ground covers that get you there: gravel, decomposed granite, pavers, concrete.

chapters.title: Zone 1 — 5 to 30 Feet: Reduce Intensity
chapters.description:
Moving outward, the objective shifts toward identifying pathways for fire to reach the house and interrupting them by reducing the amount and continuity of fuel.

Prune and separate vegetation, remove dead material and ladder fuels, and avoid dense arrangements that allow fire to move easily from grasses to shrubs, into trees and toward the home.

The goal isn't a bare landscape. It is a landscape in which fire has difficulty finding a continuous pathway.

chapters.title: Zone 2 — 30 to 100 Feet: De-energize an Approaching Fire
chapters.description:
Farther from the home, vegetation management becomes increasingly connected to the surrounding landscape.

Thin and separate fuels, manage dead vegetation and consider how trees, shrubs, fences and other combustible materials connect across property lines.

And this is where wildfire resilience begins to extend beyond your own property.

Pro Tip: Look Across the Property LineDo you share a fence, hedge, trees or vegetation with a neighbor? Zone 1 and Zone 2 often work better when adjoining properties are managed together. A coordinated project between neighbors can create more effective defensible space than either property owner can create alone.

Because at 100 feet, wildfire doesn't recognize where one parcel ends and another begins.

Neither should our planning.

media.alt: Before vegetation management: dense, unmanaged trees and shrubs close behind a Homestead property
After vegetation management: thinned and spaced vegetation with a cleared pathway on the same property
media.caption: Real before/after vegetation management on a Homestead Valley property.

chapters.navLabel: You Don't Have to Do Everything
chapters.title: You Don't Have to Do Everything
chapters.description:
Wildfire mitigation can quickly feel overwhelming.

Home hardening. Defensible space. Trees. Vents. Fences. Decks. Mulch. Windows. Evacuation.

The goal shouldn't be to do everything at once. It is to understand your vulnerabilities and prioritize. Set achievable goals — eat the elephant one bite at a time, as they say.

Every property is different, every situation is unique. A home bordering open space may have very different priorities from one surrounded by neighboring structures. A house on a steep slope may require particular attention to vegetation and fire pathways, while another may have greater vulnerability to ember entry.

Start with the conditions that could have the greatest consequence.

What could carry fire toward my home? Where could an ember enter, collect or ignite something?

Then address those vulnerabilities over time — starting with improvements that provide the greatest practical reduction in risk.

Some actions may be simple and inexpensive: clearing debris, moving combustible materials, pruning vegetation or creating separation. Others — such as replacing vents, modifying fences, upgrading windows or undertaking larger vegetation work — may require planning, investment and coordination with neighbors.

Progress matters. Each vulnerability removed is one less opportunity for fire to gain energy or an ember to become an ignition.

Pro Tip: Fix the Highest-Consequence Vulnerability FirstDon't start with the longest checklist. Start with the condition most likely to carry fire to the house or allow embers inside, then work outward from there.
Wildfire resilience isn't one project. It's a process of reducing vulnerability over time.

media.alt: Gauge dashboard showing community strengths, in-progress items and highest priorities from roughly 15,000 Homestead Valley home assessments conducted 2023-2026 by Southern Marin Fire and Firewise USA
media.caption: Real community data: about 15,000 home assessments (2023–2026) consistently show Zone 0 and common ember-entry points as the highest-priority opportunities.

chapters.title: The Next Frontier Is the Neighborhood
chapters.description:
Your home does not exist in isolation.

Fences, hedges, trees, decks, sheds and other combustible materials can create connections between properties. During wildfire, those connections can become pathways.

A burning fence can carry fire toward a neighboring structure. Vegetation can connect one property to another. And once a home ignites, the structure itself can become a powerful source of heat, flames and embers.

Individual preparedness matters — but neighborhood preparedness matters even more.

media.alt: Aerial illustration of the same hillside neighborhood showing continuous, untreated vegetation creating ignition pathways between homes, versus treated, hardened, spaced-out homes that interrupt those pathways
media.caption: Treated, spaced homes interrupt the pathways that connect one property's risk to another's.

chapters.title: Your Neighbor Can Be Part of Your Resilience
chapters.description:
It is easy to look across a property line and think: “I can do everything right and still be threatened by my neighbor.”

But there is a more useful way to think about it.

Two homeowners can create better vegetation separation along a shared boundary. Several can coordinate tree work or address a continuous fence or hedge. A group of homes can upgrade vulnerable vents, organize a cleanup day or create shared defensible space.

Individual improvements begin to reinforce one another.

Every neighborhood is different. Some Homestead homes sit on ridgelines reached by narrow, winding roads. Others are nestled in valleys or drainages. Some neighborhoods border open space; others have closely spaced homes and extensive vegetation between properties. Each has its own vulnerabilities.

So rather than asking what every neighborhood should do, ask: Where could fire gain energy in our neighborhood? Where are we collectively vulnerable to embers? Where could we interrupt the pathway together?

chapters.title: Make the Block the Unit of Action
chapters.description:
Homestead already has something many communities must create from scratch: an established Block Captain and neighborhood coordinator network.

Know your Block Captain. Make sure your block has current contact information. Know your neighbors — and whether older residents, people with limited mobility or others may need assistance preparing for or responding to an emergency.

Then consider walking the block together. Look for shared vegetation, fence lines, open-space interfaces and other conditions that may affect several properties. And choose something achievable.

One shared vulnerability. One shared project.
Pro Tip: Reach Out to Your Block Captain and Block ContactsMake sure you know who your Block Captain is, how neighbors communicate, and who on the block may need assistance before or during an emergency.

That is how resilience grows:

Home → Neighbor → Block → Neighborhood

And Homestead already has a long history of turning collective action into community results.

media.alt: Poster: when most homes in a neighborhood take action, ember pathways between homes are interrupted; about 70 percent of homes protected is the tipping point for meaningful neighborhood risk reduction
media.caption: Neighborhood participation compounds — reach out to the Safety Committee at firewise@hvlt.org to start or join an Ember Ready Neighborhood pilot.

chapters.title: Introducing the Ember Ready Initiative
chapters.description:
Homestead Valley is not doing this alone. The Marin Wildfire Prevention Authority — funded by the Measure C parcel tax that Marin voters approved in 2020 — runs the Ember Ready Initiative, a county-wide push to move mitigation from the single parcel to the shared block.

It is the same idea we have been building toward in this section, backed by regional funding, agency expertise and neighborhood-scale project support.

MWPA and Southern Marin Fire District have also invested directly in the landscape around us. Shaded fuel breaks on the Tamalpais and Homestead ridgelines are designed to give firefighters somewhere to stand and slow a fire before it reaches the built environment:

  • MWPA — Greater Mill Valley shaded fuel break public presentation (PDF)
  • Southern Marin Fire District — Tamalpais / Homestead Valley shaded fuel break (PDF)

media.caption: Kathleen Cutter — Marin Wildfire Prevention Authority, Ember Ready Initiative.

chapters.title: We've Done This Before
chapters.description:
Collective action is not new to Homestead Valley.

In fact, the community we are trying to protect exists today because earlier generations of residents chose to act together — and because of current community elders who continue to serve the community.

When development threatened Homestead's open spaces, residents organized to preserve the hillsides and natural landscape that remain central to our community today.

That tradition continued. Over the decades, residents created organizations and neighborhood networks to protect open space, strengthen emergency preparedness and reduce wildfire risk. Homestead became an early Firewise community, secured significant funding for fuels reduction and vegetation management, and developed the Block Captain and Safety Committee networks we rely on today.

More recently, partnerships with Southern Marin Fire, Marin Wildfire and other public agencies have brought additional expertise and resources to home hardening, vegetation management and neighborhood resilience.

We don't have to build a culture of collective action from scratch. We already have one.

media.caption: Jim Derich, Mark Stahl and Steve Quarles — we've done this before.

chapters.title: From Preserving Open Space to Living Resiliently Within It
chapters.description:
Our challenge today is not to choose between preserving the landscape we love and protecting ourselves from wildfire.

It is learning how to live more resiliently within that landscape.

That means applying the same spirit of collective action that helped preserve Homestead to the challenge immediately around us: our homes, our neighbors and our neighborhoods.

Pro Tip: Use the Network That Already ExistsBefore creating a new committee or program, look for an existing Homestead group, Block Captain, Safety Committee initiative or agency partner that can help move the project forward.

Previous generations showed what Homestead can accomplish when residents organize around a shared challenge.

Now it's our turn.

media.alt: Original map of Homestead Valley Land Trust's preserved open space parcels
media.caption: The original map of the open space this generation inherited — and is now building on. Source: HVLT (hvlt.org/history).

chapters.title: The Next Chapter Is Ours
chapters.description:
We began with a simple question: What does it mean to live with wildfire in Homestead Valley?

We cannot control where a fire starts, the terrain around us or which way the wind blows.

But we can influence what happens when wildfire reaches our community.

We can de-energize the pathways that allow fire to build intensity as it approaches our homes. We can harden our homes so embers have fewer opportunities to become ignitions. And we can work with our neighbors to reduce the vulnerabilities we share.

chapters.title: Start Where You Are. Help Is Available.
chapters.description:
You don't have to do everything.

Start with your home. Identify your most important vulnerabilities and address something meaningful.

Then look next door. Know your Block Captain. Talk with your neighbors. Walk your block. Look for shared vulnerabilities and opportunities to work together.

One home. One neighbor. One block. One project at a time.

Cost, physical limitations or simply not knowing where to begin can prevent people from acting. You don't have to do it alone.

Local, regional and state programs offer grants, rebates and other assistance for wildfire mitigation. These resources can be especially important for older residents, people with access or functional needs, and households for whom the cost or physical demands of the work create a barrier.

If you need help, ask for it. If you know a neighbor who may need help, reach out.

chapters.title: Resilient Neighbors. Resilient Neighborhoods.
chapters.description:
Previous generations worked together to preserve the Homestead Valley we inherited. Our challenge is to make it more resilient for the generations that follow.

We will never eliminate wildfire from the California landscape. But we can become better prepared to live with it.

We can make our homes harder to ignite. We can interrupt the pathways that connect fire to structures and properties to one another. We can help our neighbors. And we can build resilience at the scale where wildfire risk is truly shared: the neighborhood.

Understand the risk. Reduce what you can. Help your neighbor. Build resilience together.
Pro Tip: Pick One Shared ProjectDon't wait for the entire neighborhood. Find one neighbor, one shared vulnerability and one achievable project — and start there.
